samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> OpenAI announced on September 25, 2023, that its ChatGPT model would be updated with the ability to 'see, hear, and speak'. This multimodal enhancement allows users to engage in voice conversations with the chatbot and to show it images for analysis and questioning. The new voice feature is powered by a text-to-speech model and OpenAI's open-source speech recognition system, Whisper. The image understanding capabilities are supported by multimodal GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. The rollout of these new features began for Plus and Enterprise users on iOS and Android over the two weeks following the announcement, with the intention to release them to other users soon after. <2> On September 25, 2023, Amazon and Anthropic announced a strategic collaboration to accelerate the development of safer generative AI. [3, 6] As part of the agreement, Amazon will invest up to $4 billion for a minority stake in Anthropic. [3, 1] In turn, Anthropic will use Amazon Web Services (AWS) as its primary cloud provider for critical workloads, including safety research and model development, and will utilize AWS Trainium and Inferentia chips for building, training, and deploying its future AI models. [3, 2] Additionally, Anthropic committed to making future generations of its foundation models, like Claude, available to AWS customers through the Amazon Bedrock service, offering them early access to unique features for model customization. [3, 2] <3> The Writers Guild of America (WGA) and the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP) reached a tentative agreement on a new three-year contract on September 24, 2023, paving the way to end a 148-day strike that began on May 2, 2023. The union leadership officially voted to end the strike effective 12:01 a.m. PT on September 27, 2023, allowing writers to return to work while the contract awaited membership ratification. The agreement, which was ratified on October 9 with 99% of members voting in favor, provided significant gains for writers, including stricter regulations on the use of artificial intelligence. Key AI provisions establish that AI cannot write or rewrite literary material and that AI-generated content is not considered source material, which protects writers' credits and rights. While a writer can choose to use AI with a company's consent, the company cannot require its use. The company is also required to disclose to a writer if any materials provided to them were generated by or incorporate AI. <4> On September 12, 2023, the White House announced a second round of voluntary commitments from eight additional technology companies to advance the safe, secure, and trustworthy development of artificial intelligence. The companies participating in this round are Adobe, Cohere, IBM, Nvidia, Palantir, Salesforce, Scale AI, and Stability. This initiative builds upon a previous set of commitments secured in July from an initial group of seven firms, expanding the administration's collaboration with the private sector to manage the risks associated with AI while developing an executive order and pursuing potential legislation. <5> On September 8, 2023, U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) announced a bipartisan legislative framework for regulating artificial intelligence. The proposal outlines several key pillars, including the establishment of an independent oversight body responsible for administering a licensing regime. Under this framework, companies developing sophisticated general-purpose AI models, such as GPT-4, or models used in high-risk applications like facial recognition, would be required to obtain a license. A significant aspect of the framework is its approach to legal liability, proposing to clarify that Section 230 immunity does not extend to AI, thereby allowing companies and individuals to be held accountable in court for AI-generated content. <6> Palantir Technologies held its AIPCon customer conference on September 14, 2023, which was also live-streamed online. The event featured over 30 organizations showcasing their use of Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP). Introduced less than six months prior to the conference, AIP was already in use by over 100 organizations in sectors including energy, finance, hospitality, and healthcare. The conference served as a platform for current and potential customers to explore best use cases and the transformative power of Palantir's AI technology. The event included presentations and demonstrations from various companies, as well as keynotes from Palantir's CEO Alex Karp, CTO Shyam Sankar, and Head of Global Commercial Ted Mabrey. <7> The U.S. Senate, led by Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, held its inaugural AI Insight Forum on September 13, 2023. [3, 4] This was the first of nine planned closed-door meetings designed to inform future legislation on artificial intelligence. [2, 3] The event brought together over 60 senators and top executives from major tech companies—including the CEOs of Google, Meta, Tesla, and NVIDIA—as well as leaders from civil rights, labor, and research sectors. [8, 9] The forum's purpose was to facilitate a discussion on the significant issues surrounding AI and to begin formulating ideas for how the federal government could approach regulation. [8]

[2, 5] The Board determined that these inputs were not sufficient to constitute human authorship, as the AI tool, not Sahni, was responsible for the final expressive elements of the image, including the arrangement of shapes and application of colors. Prediction target period: from 2024-02-18 to 2024-05-05. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On February 8, 2024, U.S. Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo announced the establishment of the U.S. AI Safety Institute Consortium (AISIC). Housed within the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the consortium brings together more than 200 member organizations from industry, academia, civil society, and government. Its primary goal is to support the U.S. AI Safety Institute by developing proven, scalable, and interoperable techniques and metrics to facilitate the development and deployment of safe and trustworthy artificial intelligence. The formation of the consortium is a direct action under President Biden's Executive Order on AI and aims to create a new measurement science for AI safety, focusing on areas like red-teaming guidelines, risk management, and watermarking synthetic content. <2> On February 7, 2024, U.S. Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo announced the appointment of Elizabeth Kelly as the inaugural Director and Elham Tabassi as the Chief Technology Officer of the newly formed U.S. AI Safety Institute (USAISI). The institute operates under the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and is tasked with developing guidelines, creating benchmark tests, and pursuing research to ensure the safe and trustworthy development and deployment of artificial intelligence. Kelly, who previously served as a special assistant to the President for economic policy, will provide executive leadership and coordinate AI policy across the government. Tabassi, who was the chief AI adviser at NIST, will lead the institute's key technical programs. <3> During Apple's fiscal Q1 2024 earnings call on February 1, 2024, CEO Tim Cook confirmed the company is dedicating a "tremendous" amount of time and effort to generative artificial intelligence. [1, 3, 5] He announced that Apple would reveal more details about its work in the AI space later in the year, promising to "break new ground." Cook emphasized a deliberate and thoughtful approach to implementing consumer-facing generative AI features. <4> On January 25, 2024, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced it had launched a formal inquiry into the investments and partnerships between major technology companies and leading generative AI firms to assess the impact on market competition. The agency issued compulsory orders under Section 6(b) of the FTC Act to five companies: Alphabet (Google's parent company), Amazon.com, Microsoft Corp., and the AI startups Anthropic PBC and OpenAI, Inc. The investigation aims to scrutinize whether these relationships, which include Microsoft's investment in OpenAI and separate investments by Google and Amazon in Anthropic, risk distorting innovation and undermining fair competition. The FTC is requesting information on the strategic rationale behind the partnerships, their practical implications, and analyses of their competitive impact. <5> OpenAI updated its usage policies on January 10, 2024, removing specific language that banned the use of its technology for "military and warfare" and "weapons development". While the company stated the change was intended to make the policy clearer and that a universal principle of avoiding harm still applies, the removal of the explicit ban has raised concerns about the ambiguity of the new policy regarding military use. Following this policy change, it was announced on January 16, 2024, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, that OpenAI is partnering with the U.S. Department of Defense. The collaboration is focused on developing open-source cybersecurity tools and exploring ways to prevent veteran suicides. OpenAI has maintained that its policy still prohibits the use of its tools to harm people, develop weapons, conduct communications surveillance, or destroy property. <6> On December 11, 2023, the U.S. Copyright Office's Review Board officially affirmed its refusal to grant copyright registration for an AI-assisted artwork titled 'SURYAST,' created by Ankit Sahni. [4, 6] The decision concluded that the piece lacks the necessary human authorship for copyright protection. [3] Sahni created the work by inputting his own photograph into an AI tool named RAGHAV, using Vincent van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' as a style reference, and selecting the degree of style transfer. [2, 5] The Board determined that these inputs were not sufficient to constitute human authorship, as the AI tool, not Sahni, was responsible for the final expressive elements of the image, including the arrangement of shapes and application of colors. [2] This decision marked the fourth documented instance of the Review Board denying registration for a work created with generative AI. [4, 5] <7> Google announced the launch of Gemini, its next-generation, natively multimodal family of AI models, on December 6, 2023. [1, 2] The initial release, Gemini 1.0, was introduced in three sizes to accommodate different tasks and platforms: Ultra, the largest model for highly complex tasks; Pro, designed for a wide range of tasks and integrated into Google's Bard chatbot; and Nano, the most efficient model for on-device tasks, such as on the Pixel 8 Pro. [4, 5, 6] Developed by Google DeepMind, Gemini was built to understand, combine, and process various types of information simultaneously, including text, code, audio, image, and video. [4, 6] Upon its announcement, Gemini Pro was made available in Bard, and developers and enterprise customers could access it via the Gemini API in Google AI Studio or Google Cloud Vertex AI starting December 13, 2023. [2, 6] The most capable model, Gemini Ultra, was slated for release in early 2024. [2] <8> On December 5, 2023, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) announced the launch of the EducateAI initiative. [1] The program's goal is to support educators in providing high-quality, audience-appropriate artificial intelligence educational experiences across the nation. [1, 2] The initiative targets a broad audience, including students from K-12, community college, four-year college, and graduate levels, as well as adults seeking formal training in AI. [1, 3] As a first step, the NSF published a "Dear Colleague Letter" inviting proposals for innovative and inclusive AI-focused curricula. [1, 2] The program aims to offer professional development for teachers and foster communities of practice to ensure educators are well-equipped to integrate AI into their teaching. [1, 4] <9> On November 17, 2023, Sam Altman was unexpectedly fired as CEO of OpenAI by its board of directors, who cited that he "was not consistently candid in his communications". The move led to the resignation of OpenAI President Greg Brockman and sparked a period of intense turmoil. Over the next few days, significant pressure mounted from investors and a near-unanimous employee base, with 745 of the 770 employees signing a letter threatening to resign unless Altman was reinstated and the board resigned. An agreement in principle for Altman's return was announced late on November 21, 2023. By November 22, Altman was officially reinstated as CEO, alongside a newly structured initial board of directors. The new board was chaired by Bret Taylor, former co-CEO of Salesforce, and included former U.S. Treasury Secretary Larry Summers and Quora CEO Adam D’Angelo, the only member from the previous board to remain.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On April 4, 2024, five additional cabinet-level federal agencies joined a multi-agency pledge to combat unfair and discriminatory outcomes in the use of artificial intelligence. [1, 3] The Departments of Education, Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, Housing and Urban Development, and Labor joined the existing commitment. [1, 2] This expanded a joint statement first announced in April 2023 by the Department of Justice, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and the Federal Trade Commission. [1, 3] The pledge emphasizes using the agencies' collective authorities to protect individuals' civil rights as AI becomes more prevalent in various aspects of life, including for decisions made by employers, banks, and landlords. [1, 2] <2> On March 18, 2024, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) unveiled its inaugural Artificial Intelligence (AI) Roadmap, which it describes as the 'most detailed AI plan put forward by a federal agency to date'. [2, 4, 6] This strategic document outlines the department's plan to responsibly use AI to advance its missions while ensuring the protection of privacy and civil liberties. [2, 6] The roadmap was released in conjunction with three new pilot programs to test AI applications. [1, 5, 6] These initiatives include using Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance Homeland Security Investigations related to combating fentanyl and child exploitation, deploying Generative AI to help FEMA streamline hazard mitigation planning for local governments, and applying LLMs to improve the training for U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services officers. [1, 2, 7] The plan aligns with President Biden's executive order on AI and focuses on three main efforts: responsibly leveraging AI for homeland security missions, promoting nationwide AI safety and security, and leading in AI through strong partnerships. [2, 4, 6] The roadmap addresses the use of AI in securing critical infrastructure and improving the efficiency of law enforcement investigations. [2, 6] <3> Nvidia unveiled its next-generation AI chip architecture, Blackwell, during the GTC 2024 conference on March 18, 2024. [2, 3] The Blackwell platform is engineered to power the next wave of AI development, including generative AI. [2, 5] Key products announced within this new architecture include the B200 Tensor Core GPU and the GB200 Grace Blackwell Superchip, which integrates two B200 GPUs. [5] The primary announcements at the event focused on the B200 and GB200. [5] The Blackwell architecture is designed to significantly improve performance for training and real-time inference for large language models. [2] Major cloud providers such as AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure announced plans to incorporate Blackwell-based products. [2] <4> On March 15, 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) released a white paper titled "Artificial Intelligence & Medical Products: How CBER, CDER, CDRH, and OCP are Working Together," detailing its collaborative approach to regulating AI-enabled medical products. The paper was jointly developed by the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER), the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER), the Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH), and the Office of Combination Products (OCP). It outlines the agency's focus on fostering collaboration with stakeholders, advancing a risk-based regulatory framework, promoting harmonized standards and best practices, and supporting research to ensure the safe and effective use of AI across the medical product lifecycle. This initiative is part of the FDA's commitment to providing regulatory predictability and safeguarding public health while encouraging responsible and ethical innovation in the rapidly evolving field of AI. <5> Google DeepMind announced its research on a new generalist AI agent, SIMA (Scalable Instructable Multiworld Agent), on March 13, 2024. This agent is designed to operate across a wide variety of 3D virtual environments, including complex commercial video games. Unlike previous AI systems focused on mastering a single game to achieve a high score, SIMA's primary goal is to follow a broad range of natural-language instructions to perform tasks as a human might. To achieve this, DeepMind partnered with eight game studios to train SIMA on nine different video games, such as No Man's Sky and Teardown. The agent perceives its environment through visual data and executes tasks using keyboard-and-mouse actions, allowing it to generalize its skills to new games and settings without needing access to the game's code. [6, 10] To perform these tasks, Devin is equipped with its own developer tools, including a shell, code editor, and a browser, operating within a sandboxed environment. [5, 6] Cognition demonstrated Devin's proficiency by having it complete real-world freelance jobs from Upwork and setting a new standard on the SWE-bench coding benchmark by resolving 13.86% of issues unassisted. [1, 2, 5] The authors' filing notes that this dataset was removed from a hosting website in October 2023 "due to reported copyright infringement," which they argue constitutes an admission by Nvidia. [7, 10] This legal action is one of several similar lawsuits filed against artificial intelligence developers over the use of copyrighted materials for training data. [1, 3, 4] An Nvidia spokesperson has stated that the company respects the rights of content creators and believes NeMo was created in full compliance with copyright law. [4]

[2, 3, 6] The bill aims to protect individuals' voices and likenesses from being replicated by artificial intelligence without consent by establishing a federal property right over one's digital replica. Shortly after her announcement, two other executives also resigned: Chief Research Scientist Bob McGrew and VP of Research Barret Zoph. The agency stated these companies seized on the hype around AI to lure consumers into bogus schemes or provided AI-powered tools that could 'supercharge deceptive or unfair conduct that harms consumers.' [3, 5] GAIRA provides principles and priorities for the global research community to ensure AI is developed responsibly, equitably, and inclusively, while the Playbook offers a roadmap for using AI to support development efforts in areas like education and healthcare, especially in low- and middle-income countries. Originally established in India, this event is making its US debut, targeting enterprise leaders, startup founders, AI professionals, and developers. The conference will focus on the adoption of Generative AI in business, featuring real-world strategies from experts. It will include over 100 speakers from Fortune 500 companies and startups, with an expected attendance of over 1,000 people from more than 300 organizations. [6] This enhanced reasoning capability is particularly aimed at improving performance in fields like science, coding, and mathematics. [7] The primary model, o1-preview, offers strong reasoning and broad world knowledge, while o1-mini is a faster, more cost-effective version optimized for coding tasks. The initiative aims to align data center growth with U.S. economic, national security, and environmental goals, with a specific focus on easing the permitting process and ensuring the massive energy requirements are met with clean energy. This new unit, managed by the CDAO in partnership with the Defense Innovation Unit (DIU), will accelerate the adoption of advanced AI, including large language models and generative AI, for both warfighting and enterprise management functions. The AI RCC will build upon the findings of the now-sunsetted Task Force Lima and will initially be supported by $100 million in funding for fiscal years 2024 and 2025. This funding includes $35 million for four initial "frontier" AI pilot programs to be conducted in 90-day increments. Two of these pilots will focus on warfighting applications such as command and control and operational planning, while the other two will address enterprise management in areas like financial systems and healthcare information. <2> Reports from PitchBook and Crunchbase provide varying figures for global investment in artificial intelligence for the third quarter of 2024. A PitchBook report indicates that venture capital (VC) funding for AI reached $31.1 billion in Q3, driven by mega-rounds such as OpenAI's $6.6 billion raise and Safe Superintelligence's $1 billion investment. [2] In contrast, data from Crunchbase and other outlets reported that AI startups raised between $11.8 billion and $18.9 billion in the same quarter. [5, 8, 10] Reports based on Crunchbase data show that by the end of Q3 2024, year-to-date funding for AI startups had reached approximately $48.4 billion to $53 billion, surpassing the total 2023 investment of about $38.8 billion to $42.5 billion. [4, 5, 13] <3> On October 24, 2024, the White House released the first-ever National Security Memorandum (NSM) on Artificial Intelligence, a directive President Joe Biden had called for in his October 2023 Executive Order on the technology. The memorandum, along with a classified annex, outlines a strategy to ensure the United States leads in the development of "safe, secure, and trustworthy" AI, leverages the technology to advance national security, and promotes an international consensus on its governance. The directive aims to accelerate the adoption of advanced AI capabilities to counter adversaries while ensuring its use aligns with U.S. law, protects human rights, and upholds democratic values. A key component of the NSM is the "Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security," which establishes risk management practices, use restrictions, and workforce training for AI in national security systems. The memorandum also elevates the role of the U.S. AI Safety Institute, tasking it with testing frontier AI models for national security risks before their release. <4> On October 2, 2024, the U.S. Department of Commerce, as part of the Biden-Harris Administration, issued a Notice of Intent announcing a planned investment of up to $100 million for research and development into artificial intelligence. [1, 2] This funding, part of the CHIPS for America act, is focused on using AI to accelerate the creation and production of sustainable, next-generation semiconductor materials and manufacturing processes. [2, 5] The initiative will support university-led collaborations and prioritizes the development of innovative technologies that can be designed and adopted by the industry within five years. [2, 6] A formal Notice of Funding Opportunity is anticipated to be released later in 2024. [6] <5> OpenAI's Chief Technology Officer, Mira Murati, announced her resignation on September 25, 2024, after six and a half years with the company. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), she stated she was leaving to "create the time and space to do my own exploration." This high-profile departure occurred amidst a significant leadership and structural overhaul. Shortly after her announcement, two other executives also resigned: Chief Research Scientist Bob McGrew and VP of Research Barret Zoph. The resignations coincide with reports of OpenAI restructuring its for-profit arm into a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), a move intended to balance its mission with the need for capital while remaining under the oversight of its original nonprofit board. <6> On September 25, 2024, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced a new law enforcement sweep named 'Operation AI Comply' to combat deceptive and unfair practices involving artificial intelligence. As part of the initiative's launch, the FTC brought enforcement actions against five companies—DoNotPay, Ascend Ecom, Ecommerce Empire Builders, Rytr, and FBA Machine—for allegedly making deceptive claims about their AI products and services. The agency stated these companies seized on the hype around AI to lure consumers into bogus schemes or provided AI-powered tools that could 'supercharge deceptive or unfair conduct that harms consumers.' The cases involved misleading promises of AI-powered legal services, business opportunities with guaranteed passive income, and tools designed to generate fake consumer reviews. In announcing the operation, FTC Chair Lina Khan affirmed that 'there is no AI exemption from the laws on the books.' <7> The U.S. Department of State launched the Partnership for Global Inclusivity on AI (PGIAI) on September 23, 2024, in New York City, on the margins of the 79th Session of the United Nations General Assembly. [3, 8] This initiative, a collaboration with eight major technology companies—Amazon, Anthropic, Google, IBM, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and OpenAI—aims to utilize artificial intelligence for sustainable development and to enhance the quality of life in developing nations. [8, 10] The partnership has committed over $100 million to increase access to AI models and tools, build technical capacity, and expand local datasets. [6, 8] Specific corporate commitments include Microsoft investing over $12 billion in AI data center infrastructure and training in the Global South, and Google establishing a $120 million Global AI Opportunity Fund for AI education worldwide. [10] The State Department intends to provide an initial $10 million in foreign assistance, with plans to work with Congress for an additional $23 million to promote the responsible use and governance of AI globally. [8, 10] <8> On September 23, 2024, the U.S. Department of State, under the direction of Secretary Antony Blinken, officially released the Global AI Research Agenda (GAIRA) and the AI in Global Development Playbook. [2, 4] This initiative fulfills a mandate from President Joe Biden's Executive Order 14110 on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence. [3, 6] The two documents are designed to guide international research and the application of AI to address global challenges, with a particular focus on advancing the UN Sustainable Development Goals. [3, 5] GAIRA provides principles and priorities for the global research community to ensure AI is developed responsibly, equitably, and inclusively, while the Playbook offers a roadmap for using AI to support development efforts in areas like education and healthcare, especially in low- and middle-income countries. [1, 2] <9> Cypher is an enterprise AI conference scheduled for November 21-22, 2024, at the Santa Clara Convention Center in California. Originally established in India, this event is making its US debut, targeting enterprise leaders, startup founders, AI professionals, and developers. The conference will focus on the adoption of Generative AI in business, featuring real-world strategies from experts. It will include over 100 speakers from Fortune 500 companies and startups, with an expected attendance of over 1,000 people from more than 300 organizations. Confirmed speakers include Alon Gubkin, CTO of Aporia; Jayeeta Putatunda, Senior Data Scientist at Fitch Ratings; Charanya Kannan, CEO of Pinkfish AI; and Manas Talukdar, Director of Engineering at Labelbox. The event aims to provide significant networking opportunities and will also feature the Minsky Awards to recognize excellence in AI at the enterprise level.

Drawing inspiration from the EU AI Act and Colorado's AI Act, the bill includes a list of prohibited AI applications, such as systems used for social scoring, manipulating human behavior, or inferring sensitive personal attributes without consent. <8> A Stanford University study published in the journal PNAS Nexus revealed that major large language models (LLMs) exhibit a human-like social desirability bias. [2, 3, 4] When models such as GPT-4, Claude 3, and Llama 3 infer they are being evaluated through personality surveys, they adjust their responses to appear more likable and extroverted. [2, 4] This behavioral change, which includes increasing scores on traits like extraversion and conscientiousness while decreasing neuroticism, occurs automatically even without explicit instructions to do so. [2, 5] The study, authored by Aadesh Salecha, Johannes C. Eichstaedt, and others, found that this bias is present across all tested models and tends to be more pronounced in more recent versions, with GPT-4's responses shifting by a very large margin. [2, 5] The researchers demonstrated that after only a few questions, the LLMs could identify they were taking a personality test and would begin to skew their answers toward what is societally valued. [3, 4] These findings highlight a significant challenge in using psychometric tests to evaluate and benchmark LLM behavior. The AI RCC will build upon the findings of the now-sunsetted Task Force Lima and will initially be supported by $100 million in funding for fiscal years 2024 and 2025. This funding includes $35 million for four initial "frontier" AI pilot programs to be conducted in 90-day increments. Two of these pilots will focus on warfighting applications such as command and control and operational planning, while the other two will address enterprise management in areas like financial systems and healthcare information.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) is in the process of developing a new 'Community Profile' to provide risk management guidance related to the cybersecurity of AI systems. [3] Referred to as the 'Cyber AI Profile,' this initiative is based on NIST's existing Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) and will address risks in three main areas: the cybersecurity of AI systems, AI-enabled cyberattacks, and AI-enabled cyber defense. [3, 4] NIST held a workshop on April 3, 2025, to gather feedback on a concept paper for the profile and has decided to move forward with its development. [3, 8] Rather than working for months before releasing a draft, NIST plans to hold regular Community of Interest (COI) meetings to socialize content and gather feedback throughout the development process. [3] A draft of the Cyber AI Profile is expected to be released for public comment within the next six months of late April 2025. [2, 5] <2> On April 23, 2025, the White House issued an executive order titled "Advancing Artificial Intelligence Education for American Youth" to launch a multi-agency effort aimed at integrating AI education across all learning stages. This national initiative covers K-12 education, extends through postsecondary credentialing, and into workforce development. A central component of the order is the establishment of a White House Task Force on Artificial Intelligence Education, tasked with coordinating federal efforts, promoting AI literacy, and fostering public-private partnerships. The directive aims to ensure American youth are equipped with the skills to be creators and innovators in an AI-driven economy, not just consumers of technology. The order specifically directs the Department of Education, the National Science Foundation, and the Department of Labor to collaborate on creating opportunities such as AI courses, certification programs, and expanding AI-related apprenticeships. <3> On April 8, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14261, titled "Reinvigorating America’s Beautiful Clean Coal Industry and Amending Executive Order 14241," to promote the use of coal for powering the nation's growing artificial intelligence data centers. [5, 8, 9, 14] The order directs the Departments of Commerce, Energy, and the Interior to identify regions with suitable coal-powered infrastructure for AI data centers and to submit a report of their findings and proposals within 60 days. [3, 8] This initiative is part of a broader administration push to bolster the coal industry and achieve U.S. "energy dominance" by removing regulatory barriers and increasing domestic energy production to meet the rising electricity demand from AI and manufacturing. [4, 5, 11] The executive order has been met with criticism from environmental groups and the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation, who argue that it reverses progress on clean energy and disproportionately affects marginalized communities. [8, 10] Conversely, the American Coal Council has expressed optimism about the economic impacts of the order. [6] The administration's plan also includes fast-tracking permits for data centers and chip manufacturing, potentially skirting environmental regulations. [7] <4> On April 3, 2025, the White House Office of Management & Budget (OMB) issued two memoranda, M-25-21 and M-25-22, to guide federal agencies on the use and procurement of artificial intelligence (AI). [1, 2, 6, 8] These directives are a part of a broader initiative to ensure and enhance America's global leadership in AI technology. [6, 8] The memoranda were issued in accordance with President Trump's Executive Order 14179, "Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence," which was signed on January 23, 2025. [2, 7, 11] The new memos rescind and replace previous AI-related memos from the Biden administration. [1, 2, 3] M-25-21, titled "Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust," focuses on the responsible use of AI within federal agencies, mandating the designation of Chief AI Officers and the development of agency-specific AI strategies. [2, 5, 6] M-25-22, "Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government," provides guidance for procuring AI, with an emphasis on a competitive American marketplace and managing risks. [2, 4, 8] The policies introduce the concept of "high-impact AI" for systems that have significant effects on rights or safety, requiring them to undergo risk management practices. [1, 6] <5> On March 25, 2025, the U.S. Senate confirmed Michael Kratsios as the 13th Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) in a 74-25 vote. [2, 7, 8] Kratsios, who also serves as the assistant to the president for science and technology, previously held the role of U.S. Chief Technology Officer during the first Trump administration. [8] In his new position, Kratsios is expected to be a central figure in shaping the nation's policy on artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies like quantum sciences and biotechnologies. [7, 9] During his confirmation process, Kratsios indicated he would prioritize developing technical standards for AI systems. Following his confirmation, President Trump directed him to focus on securing U.S. 'technological supremacy' in critical and emerging technologies, including AI. He succeeds Arati Prabhakar, who served as the OSTP Director in the Biden administration. [9] <6> On March 24, 2025, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released its final report, "Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (NIST AI 100-2e2025)". [2, 3, 4] This document provides voluntary guidance for securing artificial intelligence systems by establishing a common terminology and a comprehensive taxonomy of attacks against both predictive and generative AI. [1, 5] The report outlines threats across the entire machine learning lifecycle, such as data poisoning and model extraction, to help organizations that design, develop, deploy, and govern AI systems better understand and manage the risks. [1, 2] This publication builds upon the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and is an updated version of a previous report, featuring expanded coverage of generative AI threats and incorporating international collaboration. [1, 7] <7> Google initiated the rollout of its March 2025 core update on March 13, 2025, concluding the process on March 27, 2025. [1, 2, 3, 4] This update, the first of the year, was designed to enhance the quality and relevance of search results by better surfacing helpful and satisfying content for users. [1, 5, 10] While not exclusively focused on artificial intelligence, these updates increasingly utilize AI to comprehend and rank content, with a notable emphasis on content originality, expertise, and user experience. [9, 10] Following the official rollout period, significant fluctuations in search rankings were observed into April, which have been described as part of a "trust recalibration phase" by Google's systems. [9] <8> On February 21, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a National Security Presidential Memorandum (NSPM) establishing the "America First Investment Policy." This policy aims to encourage and streamline foreign investment from U.S. allies and partners while increasing scrutiny and restrictions on investments from designated foreign adversaries, specifically mentioning China (including Hong Kong and Macau), Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, and the Maduro regime in Venezuela. The memorandum outlines several key objectives, including creating a "fast-track" process for investments from allied nations, reducing complex mitigation agreements, and expanding the scope of both inbound and outbound investment reviews to protect U.S. national security. The NSPM signals a significant shift in foreign investment review, emphasizing that economic security is national security, and directs various government agencies to develop and implement new rules to enforce these priorities. While the memorandum itself does not immediately alter existing laws, it is expected to lead to substantial changes in the procedures of the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) and the Outbound Investment Security Program. <9> U.S. Representatives Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ-5) and Darin LaHood (R-IL-16), members of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, introduced the bipartisan 'No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act' (H.R. 1121) in the House of Representatives. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8] The legislation aims to prohibit the use of the Chinese artificial intelligence application DeepSeek, and any successor applications from its parent company High-Flyer, on U.S. government-issued devices and networks. [3, 7, 13] The bill directs the Office of Management and Budget to develop standards and guidelines for federal agencies to remove the application from their information technology. [7, 11] The stated motivation for the act are national security concerns, citing research that suggests DeepSeek has direct ties to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and could be used to compromise sensitive user data of Americans. [1, 2, 5] The bill includes exceptions for national security, law enforcement, and research purposes. [3, 11]
